title: “Kindness and Firmness”:
subtitle: Negotiating Empire in the Benjamin O’Fallon Delegation

items.abstract: <jats:p><span>Artificial intelligence is moving from systems that primarily generate outputs toward systems that can plan, use tools, modify state and take actions on behalf of users. This transition is often described as a move from automation to autonomy, but this paper argues that delegation is the more useful unit of analysis. Traditional automation encodes a process in advance; delegation transfers a bounded portion of judgement about how an objective should be achieved. The paper proposes a Delegation Spectrum ranging from passive tools to persistent delegated agents and introduces the Authority Envelope: a framework for analysing what an agent is allowed to decide, which tools and data it may access, how long its authority persists, what external effects it may create, and when it must escalate to a human. It further develops a Delegation-Risk Gradient based on authority, uncertainty, irreversibility, persistence and external reach. The paper argues that the economic significance of AI agents will depend less on whether systems can act than on whether organisations can safely transfer bounded judgement to them. Identity, permissions, reversibility, evaluation, interoperability and accountability therefore become as important as raw model capability. The central claim is that the unit of automation is the task; the unit of delegation is the authority envelope.</span></jats:p>
title: AI Agents and the Delegation Economy: From Automation to Autonomous Action

items.abstract: <jats:p>The Human Delegation Provenance (HDP) protocol establishes a cryptographic framework for verifying that AI agent actions were legitimately delegated by a human principal. HDP was designed for software agentic systems operating in digital environments. This companion specification, HDP-P, extends the HDP trust model to physical AI agents: robots, autonomous vehicles, surgical systems, and other embodied systems capable of taking irreversible actions in the physical world. HDP-P introduces new delegation claim types, embodiment constraints, irreversibility classifications, and a physical action authorization protocol that composes with HDP's existing token model. We define a threat model specific to physical AI orchestration pipelines, identify four classes of attack not addressed by current frameworks, and propose protocol extensions to close these gaps. The central contribution is the Irreversibility Class system (Class 0 through Class 3), which mandates pre-execution authorization verification rather than post-hoc audit for actions that cannot be undone. HDP-P is intended for adoption by robotics orchestration platforms, physical AI infrastructure providers, and standards bodies addressing embodied agent safety.</jats:p>

<jats:p>Frontier AI models are becoming more capable, but enterprise incidents from AI agents need not decline. This paper explains why. When firms delegate tasks to AI agents, capability improvements reduce the failure risk of fixed tasks, but governance-constrained firms expand delegated authority until their incident-absorption capacity binds again. The result is delegation risk homeostasis: incident intensity per unit of agent-task exposure can remain stable even as models improve. The model also predicts severity drift, because constant-frequency incidents migrate into higher-authority tasks, and release-cycle overshoot, because firms may expand authority faster than field performance is learned. The framework identifies the underwriting objects for AI agent liability insurance: governance capacity, exposure volume, delegated authority, control quality, release-window risk, and claim-layer containment. The implication is not that model quality is irrelevant, but that model generation alone is not a sufficient rating variable.</jats:p>
title: Delegation Risk Homeostasis:&nbsp;Why More Capable AI Agents Need Not Produce Fewer Incidents
